catalog_quote: A root in Kaytetye has one prominence. The stress pattern in Kaytetye roots is conditioned to whether the word is consonant-initial (Turpin & Ross 2012: 26). If the word is consonant-initial, this prominence is always on the initial vowel (62). Kayte [ˈkai.tə] ‘Grub.’ If the word is vowel-initial, the second vowel is stressed. Aleke [aˈlə.kə] ‘Dog.’ If there is an initial long vowel, i.e. /ɐː/, the initial vowel is stressed. Aherre /ɐ:rə/ → [ˈaː.rə] ‘Kangaroo.’ Polysyllabic suffixes show the same stress pattern. For example, fieldworkers agree that in the word in (65), there is a prominence in both the noun root and the proprietive suffix. Alek-akake dog-PROP [aˈlə.kaˌka.kə] ‘Having a dog.’ ... [pp.124-125] the first syllable with an onset in a lexical root receives stress (Turpin & Ross 2012: 26). Artetye [a.ˈʈə.cə] ‘Mulga.’ Taltye [ˈtal.cə] ‘Raindrop.’ ... a single stress assignment rule can be applied in both simplex and complex word forms: Assign a stress to the first consonant-initial syllable in a prosodic word (Goedemans 1996; Topintzi & Nevins 2017; Turpin & Ross 2012: 26). ... [p.209-210] The standard surface pattern of Kaytetye stress is that the first vowel preceded by a consonant is stressed. ... there is no evidence for feet in Kaytetye. This is because: (i) Kaytetye does not have secondary stress on monomorphemic roots; (ii) All facts of Kaytetye stress are accounted for without appealing to the existence of feet.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kaytetye is not in the catalog. The single title-works with stress in the title, Turpin 2007 'Artfully hidden' (Musicology Australia 29: 93-108, doi 10.1080/08145857.2007.10416590), is a song-rhythm/text-setting study of the Akwelye song series, not a word-stress description; it is paywalled at Taylor & Francis with no open copy (Unpaywall is_oa=false, Semantic Scholar CLOSED with abstract elided, archive.org 0 hits, Sydney eScholarship 403; Low acquisition priority: the same authors' open AMP 2021 paper (held by the project) already states the stress rule the song analyses use. The best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Panther 2021 (PhD, Newcastle; held by the project) s.3.5.1 pp. 80-81 and s.5.4.1 p. 124: one prominence per root on the first consonant-initial syllable (C-initial words sigma-1, V-initial words sigma-2), initial-/ɐː/ roots excepted, polysyllabic suffixes as separate stress domains, no feet. Corroborated by Koch 1980 p. 266 rule (18), San & Turpin 2021 p. 2, Breen 2001 p. 55 (Arandic-wide) and Harvey et al. 2023 p. 39 (consensus tonic = first medial vowel). If Kaytetye is added to the catalog, Panther 2021 is the recommended deciding source and the system is onset-conditioned (not length-conditioned). all lookups were by direct API/URL probes.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable that has an onset consonant: initial syllable in consonant-initial words, second syllable in (short-)vowel-initial words; i.e. the first vowel following a consonant is stressed. Onset-sensitive fixed stress at the left edge of the prosodic word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Panther 2021 (s.6.3.3.1, ch.8; echoed by Harvey et al. 2023: 52): no secondary stress on monomorphemic roots and no evidence for metrical feet; additional prominences arise only because polysyllabic suffixes and second constituents of complex words (e.g. Alek-akake [aˈlə.kaˌka.kə], Associated Path auxiliaries) form their own prosodic words, each stressed on its first onsetful syllable. San & Turpin 2021 instead describe left-to-right trochaic footing from the first onsetful syllable. Koch 1997: 285 notes Arandic languages mostly lack the common Australian penultimate secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Roots with an initial long vowel /ɐː/ (e.g. aherre [ˈaːrə] 'kangaroo', historically from loss of a velar glide per Breen 2001: 55) take stress on the initial vowel (Panther 2021: 81, 123 fn.17). Word-final vowels cannot be stressed (San & Turpin 2021: 2). Initial and final vowels are variably dropped in colloquial speech, which does not move the stress off the first post-consonantal vowel. Clitics do not receive independent stress (Panther 2021 s.5.4.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word = root or polysyllabic affix (Panther 2021: 82, 124); complex words contain several prosodic words each with its own stress. Statements are based on citation/elicited forms transcribed by fieldworkers plus the kPhon acoustic database (Panther's Table 37 counts stressed vs unstressed transcriptions of initial #ɐ vs #ɐː). Same rule stated independently by Koch 1980: 266 (rule 18: V -> stressed / #(V)C __), Koch 1997: 285, Breen 2001: 55 (Arandic-wide), San & Turpin 2021: 2, Harvey et al. 2023: 39.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Kaytetye proper (kayt1238; older spellings Kaititj (Koch 1980), Kaytej (Koch 1984/1990)). Breen 2001 p.55, Koch 1997 p.285 and Harvey et al. 2023 p.39 state the rule for the Arandic group as a whole (aran1266), of which Kaytetye is a member; Panther 2021, San & Turpin 2021 and Koch 1980 state it for Kaytetye specifically. Note Glottolog's list for kayt1238 includes Capell 1953 'Waramunga', which is a different language (Warumungu) and was not pursued.

sources.quote: The stress rule, formalised in (18), assigns stress to the vowel that follows the first consonant position in a word. (18) V → stressed / #(V)C. This means that a word beginning with a consonant (cluster) is stressed on the first syllable, e.g. [two examples, scanned-garbled], while vowel-initial words receive stress on the second syllable, e.g. [two examples, scanned-garbled].

sources.citation: San, Nay & Myfany Turpin (2021). Text-setting in Kaytetye. Proceedings of the 2020 Annual Meeting on Phonology (AMP 9). doi:10.3765/amp.v9i0.4911
sources.quote: Kaytetye has fixed stress, like many Australian languages. Unlike most Australian languages, however, Kaytetye has word-initial vowels. Stress assignment in Kaytetye is onset-sensitive and footing proceeds trochaically from left to right starting with the first syllable with an onset, e.g. a(ˈlə.kə) 'dog' vs. (ˈku.ɾə) 'girl'; word final vowels can not be stressed, e.g. *[ˈku.ɾɪmˈbə]. Thus, in Kaytetye, the word-initial onsetless syllable can never be stressed
sources.note: p.2: 'Kaytetye has fixed word stress which is invariably placed on the first syllable of a word with an onset'; 'Stress assignment in Kaytetye is onset-sensitive and footing proceeds trochaically from left to right starting with the first syllable with an onset, e.g. a(ˈlə.kə) 'dog' vs. (ˈku.ɾə) 'girl'; word final vowels can not be stressed'; the word-initial onsetless syllable can never be stressed.

sources.quote: The most widespread stress rule in Arandic, usually stated: main stress falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant, does not have a simple statement in terms of conventional syllables, but is: stress falls on the second syllable with VC(C) syllables.
sources.note: p.55 (Arandic-wide): 'The most widespread stress rule in Arandic, usually stated: main stress falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant.. is: stress falls on the second syllable with VC(C) syllables.' s.4.5 Kaytetye (pp.59-61) treats vowels/prepalatalisation only, no Kaytetye-specific stress rule.

sources.note: Acoustic study of word stress (one speaker, isolated words): stressed vowels have higher F0 and intensity; pitch is treated only as a correlate of stress, nothing on lexical tone.

tone.quote: Results indicate that the stressed vowels are produced with a significantly higher pitch (F0) and intensity (see Figure 3). Interestingly, the magnitude of these differences between stressed and unstressed vowels are more pronounced in long words than in short words. Significant differences were found for F1 and duration between stress conditions only in long words. … For the present study, it is difficult to ascertain whether these findings are a result of lexical or phrasal stress, as the words were produced in isolation for the dictionary

tone.quote: Rather than the position of stress shifting in these words, the duration of the first CV syllable has been shortened and so the following syllable appears to assume the stressed position. Initial observations suggest pitch and intensity rather than duration are the cues to stress. Verification of such a proposal would require extensive acoustic analysis.
